AGA Clinical Practice Update on Surveillance of Metaplastic and Premalignant Conditions of the Esophagus and Colorectum in Older Adults
  • Source: Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2026 (Vol. ■, Iss. ■)
  • Topic: Endoscopic surveillance of Barrett's esophagus and colorectal polyps/cancer in adults >75 years
  • Authors: Calderwood AH, Yoshida CM, Das KK, Falk GW
1. Aging Population Context
  • US adults ≥65 will reach 82 million by 2050 (23% of population)
  • This group growing 5× faster than total population
  • Healthcare providers increasingly need to discuss cessation of cancer screening
1.1 Life Expectancy Data
  • US life expectancy: 81.1 years (women), 75.8 years (men)
  • 10-year life expectancy needed to derive survival benefit from cancer screening
  • Age alone is insufficient marker of prognosis in older adults
1.2 Frailty Considerations
  • Frailty = physiological decline in reserve and function
  • Associated with ↑ vulnerability to adverse health outcomes/death
  • Reduced tolerance to medical/surgical interventions
  • A frail 70-year-old may have shorter life expectancy than a robust 85-year-old
2. Barrett's Esophagus Surveillance
2.1 Definition & Prevalence
  • BE = intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus
  • 2%–7% prevalence in general population
2.2 Progression Risk (Annual)
  • Nondysplastic BE (∼90% of BE population): 0.1%–0.3%/year
  • Low-grade dysplasia: 2.2%–11.8%/year for HGD/EAC
  • 5-year risk of cancer: 3.46%/year
  • Overwhelming majority of BE patients will never develop adenocarcinoma
2.3 Competing Mortality in BE
  • Patients with BE largely die of causes other than adenocarcinoma:
  • Cardiovascular disease
  • Pulmonary diseases
  • Other cancers
  • After successful endoscopic therapy for BE-related neoplasia:
  • Other-cause mortality is 40× higher than esophageal adenocarcinoma mortality
  • Strongly predicted by Charlson Comorbidity Index
2.4 Surveillance Goal
  • Detect dysplasia and adenocarcinoma at early, treatable stage
  • Allows for endoscopic eradication therapy
  • Avoids need for invasive surgery
2.5 Evidence for Surveillance Benefit
  • Observational studies show improved survival in surveillance-detected vs nonsurveillance-detected esophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Earlier stage disease
  • Lower tumor grade
  • ↓ cancer-related mortality
  • Recent RCT (UK, BOSS trial) showed no difference in:
  • Overall survival
  • Cancer-specific survival
  • Time to diagnosis of EAC
  • Cancer stage with every 2-year surveillance vs endoscopy for symptoms only
  • Study limitations: many without intestinal metaplasia, more frequent endoscopy than guideline recommended
2.6 Quality Indicators for Surveillance Endoscopy
  • Current guidelines recommend specific protocols
  • Adherence to best practice biopsy protocols is variable
  • Nonadherence associated with ↓ detection of dysplasia
  • May contribute to post-endoscopy esophageal adenocarcinoma
2.7 When to Stop BE Surveillance
2.7.1 Age-Based Recommendations
  • 2025 AGA Guideline: Initiate conversation about discontinuing at age 75 (healthy men)
  • ESGE Guideline: Last surveillance at 75, with individual exceptions up to 80
2.7.2 Optimal Age Range (Cost-Effectiveness Analysis)
  • Depends on sex and comorbidities
  • Optimal age ranges from:
  • 69 years (women with severe comorbidities)
  • 81 years (men without comorbidities)
2.7.3 Absolute Cessation Criteria
  • Inability to tolerate endoscopic therapy, surgery, or oncologic interventions for esophageal adenocarcinoma --> cessation regardless of age
  • Anticipated survival <5 years
  • Multiple comorbidities
2.8 Risk Stratification Tools for BE
2.8.1 PIB (Progression in Barrett's Esophagus) Score
  • Validated model to predict progression to high-grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma
  • Incorporates clinical, endoscopic, and histologic variables from baseline endoscopy
  • Potential to inform patients of estimated risk of progression
  • 2025 AGA guideline did not endorse its use
2.8.2 Machine Learning Models
  • Applied to electronic health records to predict EAC risk
  • Show promise and better performance than PIB
  • Require external validation
2.8.3 Molecular Biomarkers
  • p53 abnormalities most studied to date
  • Can support diagnosis of dysplasia and assessment of atypia on biopsies
  • Cannot prognosticate cancer risk in nondysplastic BE
2.8.4 Tissue Systems Pathology Test
  • Immunofluorescence staining of 9 protein-based biomarkers
  • Nuclear pathology + tissue architecture from standard histologic biopsies
  • Quantitative image analysis
  • Sensitivity/specificity for high-risk classifications:
  • High risk: 38% sensitivity, 94% specificity
  • High/intermediate risk: 55% sensitivity, 82% specificity
  • 2022 AGA update suggests use for risk stratification in nondysplastic BE
  • 2025 AGA guideline makes no recommendation (for or against)
3. Colorectal Cancer Screening in Older Adults
3.1 Guideline Recommendations by Age
  • 75–85 years: Individualize decision to pursue screening
  • >85 years: Stop screening (US guidelines)
  • Despite guidance, colonoscopy frequently performed in patients with <10-year life expectancy
3.2 Benefits of CRC Screening
  • Prevent CRC death and morbidity
  • Provide peace of mind
3.2.1 Risk After Prior Normal Screening
  • Patients with prior normal colonoscopy or stool-based tests have lower CRC risk than general population:
  • 2 years: 0.39% (colonoscopy) vs 0.23% (stool test)
  • 8 years: 1.29% vs 1.21%
3.2.2 Yield in Age 76–85
  • Majority have normal or nonsignificant findings (e.g., nonadvanced adenomas)
  • Only 0.2%–0.5% diagnosed with CRC
  • Advanced adenomas found in 6%–8%
  • Questionable whether advanced adenomas will cause harm within patients' lifetimes
3.3 Harms of CRC Screening Colonoscopy
  • 14–28 per 1000 in older adults (vs younger patients)
  • 1.7× higher than in patients <60 years
  • Risks ↑ for every 5 years >75 years of age
  • ↑ risk with more comorbidities, antithrombotic agents, shorter life expectancy
3.3.1 Harms by Category
  • Non-GI harms (arrhythmia, aspiration pneumonia, MI, ischemic stroke) exceed GI-related harms
  • GI harms: bleeding and perforation
3.3.2 Risk-Benefit Balance
  • Harms of colonoscopy (∼26 per 1000) likely outweigh benefits of finding CRC (2–3 per 1000)
  • Need to carefully select patients with longer life expectancy for screening after age 75
3.4 Impact of Comorbidities on Screening Benefit
  • In cohort study, screening endoscopy after 75 in patients with significant comorbidities:
  • Not associated with reduction in CRC death
  • Associated with ↑ non–CRC-related mortality and all-cause mortality
4. Colorectal Polyp Surveillance in Older Adults
4.1 US Guidance Gap
  • Absence of definitive stopping ages for surveillance
  • Contributed to overuse of surveillance colonoscopy
4.2 Risk by Polyp History (Age >75)
4.2.1 Low-Risk Adenomas
  • Definition: 1–2 small (<1 cm) adenomas without villous features or high-grade dysplasia
  • 5-year CRC risk: ∼0.5%
  • Risk similar to those without adenomas
  • Lower than general population
4.2.2 Advanced Adenomas
  • Higher lifetime risk of future neoplasia
  • Estimated 5-year CRC risk: 0.8%
4.2.3 Serial Surveillance Findings
  • Baseline advanced adenomas → low-risk adenomas at first surveillance:
  • High-risk adenomas at second surveillance: 3%–24.3%
  • Baseline advanced → no adenomas at first surveillance:
  • High-risk adenomas at second surveillance: 4%–12.3%
4.3 Competing Mortality
  • Rates of incident CRC and CRC death far surpassed by competing mortality from non-CRC death:
  • ∼22% at 5 years
  • ∼48% at 10 years
  • Suggests older adults can deprioritize surveillance colonoscopy relative to other health concerns
5. Decision-Making Tools & Frameworks
5.1 Prognostic Calculators
  • Lee–Schonberg Index: Most widely used, well-validated tool
  • Estimates life expectancy using age, frailty/function, comorbidity
  • Predicts 4-to-14-year mortality
  • Available online (ePrognosis Colorectal Cancer Screening Prognostic Calculator)
  • Generate individual risk profiles to support cancer screening decisions
5.2 Frailty Assessment Tools
  • eFrailty tool: https://efrailty.hsl.harvard.edu/index.html
5.3 Patient Decision Aids (PDAs)
  • Incorporate graphics tailored to individual health status
  • Help patients decide whether to continue cancer screening
  • ePrognosis Colorectal Cancer Screening Prognostic Calculator includes PDA features
5.4 Communication Strategies
  • Provider scripts help clinicians initiate discussions and promote patient engagement
  • Core principles:
  • Emphasize shared decision-making anchored in patient goals/preferences
  • Reference age-/health-based guidelines
  • Focus on potential harms outweighing benefits
  • Frame stopping as appropriate care; normalize recommendation
  • Avoid language focusing on old age, life expectancy
  • Reassure patients they can still have testing if new symptoms develop
5.5 Decision Framework for BE Surveillance
  • Can patient tolerate endoscopic/surgical/oncologic intervention for esophageal cancer?
  • NO --> Harms > Benefits → Stop surveillance
  • Life expectancy >5 years?
  • NO --> Harms > Benefits → Stop surveillance
  • Benefits > Harms? (discuss face-to-face with GI/PCP no later than age 75)
  • Consider deprioritizing at age 80 in otherwise healthy patients
5.6 Decision Framework for Colonoscopy (Screening/Surveillance)
  • Prior screening or high-quality colo? → YES/NO branches
  • Life expectancy >10 years?
  • History of advanced polyp? → YES/NO branches
  • Each branch leads to: Benefits > Harms or Harms > Benefits
  • Face-to-face discussion with GI/PCP close to surveillance due date
6. Noninvasive CRC Screening Alternatives in Older Adults
6.1 Advantages
  • No direct harms to patients
  • Risk-stratify those with positive test who are more likely to benefit from colonoscopy
  • Limit harms among majority with negative test
6.2 Performance Considerations by Age
  • Specificity of noninvasive tests decreases with age
  • Can drop to as low as 80% → higher false positivity rates
  • Therefore, FIT (fecal immunochemical test) may be preferred over other noninvasive modalities in older adults
6.3 FIT Performance
  • Performs well across all ages
  • Preferred strategy when minimizing unnecessary colonoscopy is priority
6.4 Other Noninvasive Tests
  • Multitarget stool DNA (Cologuard, Cologuard Plus)
  • Stool RNA testing (Colosense)
  • Blood-based tests (Guardant Shield, Freenome cell-free DNA test)
6.5 Important Caveat
  • Any older patient considering CRC screening with noninvasive strategy must be willing and healthy enough to undergo colonoscopy if test is positive
7. Adverse Events by Age
7.1 Colonoscopy Risk by Age
  • Overall risks in patients >65 are almost 22-fold higher than younger adults
  • Risk ↑ for every 5 years >75 regardless of indication
7.2 Upper Endoscopy Risk
  • Cardiopulmonary adverse events more common in patients ≥65
  • Higher risk with concomitant diseases:
  • Coronary artery disease
  • Hypertension
  • Diabetes
  • Obesity
  • Higher ASA scores and frailty → ↑ risk of serious adverse events
8. Documentation & Communication Requirements
8.1 Electronic Health Record Documentation
  • Clinical decision-making process for colonoscopy should be clearly documented in EHR for individuals >75 years
8.2 Transition Recommendations
  • Transition away from open-access colonoscopy in adults >75
8.3 Specialty Communication
  • Decision-making should include communication across specialties (e.g., via e-consult)
  • PCPs may contact gastroenterologists to understand patient's CRC risk
  • Gastroenterologists may contact PCPs for overall health information
8.4 Patient Preferences to Elicit
  • Whether patients could/would pursue treatment (e.g., colectomy, chemotherapy) if CRC diagnosed
  • In patients >75 undergoing colonoscopy: 10 of 15 found to have CRC did not pursue treatment
9. Overutilization Issues
9.1 BE Surveillance Overuse
  • Documented in Medicare and other populations
  • Endoscopists systematically undersample patients with long-segment BE
9.2 Colonoscopy Overuse in Older Adults
  • Documented based on:
  • Low-risk indications (screening, low-risk polyp surveillance)
  • Limited potential benefit (patients with multiple comorbidities)
9.3 Barriers to Stopping Surveillance
  • Standing recall systems
  • PCP defaults to prior colonoscopy recommendations
  • Colonoscopy reports written without knowledge of patient's future health

10.3 Competing Mortality
  • Risk of death from other causes vs specific cancer: 97–210× higher (CRC)
  • Risk of death from other causes vs EAC: 10× higher
11. Research Gaps & Future Directions
11.1 Needed Evidence
  • Real-world effectiveness and cost-effectiveness analysis in diverse populations
  • Studies on deimplementation of colonoscopy in older adults
  • Long-term risk of CRC across serial surveillance exams
11.2 Model Refinements Needed
  • Existing models would benefit from data on:
  • Serial colonoscopy results
  • Impact on CRC incidence
  • Impact on CRC mortality and all-cause mortality in older adults
11.3 Ongoing Studies
  • COOP Study: Evaluating noninvasive tests (FIT) for polyp surveillance in older adults with history of adenomas
